meta.title: Choosing a prior
reference.title: Further reading
reference.text: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., CRC Press, 2013, chapters 1–2.
content.0: A prior describes uncertainty about a parameter before considering the current data. It can use previous studies, subject knowledge or practical constraints; its implications should be checked on the scale of the problem.
content.2: An informative prior concentrates probability in a narrower region. A weakly informative prior rules out or downweights implausible values while allowing a wide range. A noninformative prior attempts to contribute relatively little information, but its properties depend on the parameterization and problem.
content.3: Some noninformative priors are improper: their densities do not integrate to one. Such a prior can only be used for posterior inference when the resulting posterior is proper.
content.5: With the same data, 8 successes in 10 trials, a $\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$ prior produces a $\operatorname{Beta}(9,3)$ posterior with mean $0.75$. A $\operatorname{Beta}(10,10)$ prior produces $\operatorname{Beta}(18,12)$ with mean $0.6$. The more concentrated second prior has a stronger influence on this small sample.
content.6:
p <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 500)
plot(p, dbeta(p, 9, 3), type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Probability of success", ylab = "Posterior density")
lines(p, dbeta(p, 18, 12), col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("Beta(1,1) prior", "Beta(10,10) prior"),
       col = c("black", "steelblue"), lwd = 2)
content.7: Comparing reasonable priors is a sensitivity analysis. If conclusions change substantially, report that dependence and consider what additional information could help choose a prior.
